summary:
Summary
A lander at the lunar south pole needs two things to survive and work: sunlight for power and a line of
sight to Earth for communication. Near the pole the Sun skims the horizon and long shadows are
everywhere, and Earth can sit just above or below the horizon depending on the site. Choosing a site is
therefore a trade-off.
Lunar Site Advisor is a simple web tool that answers one question for mission planners: which of these
sites is best, and in which weeks of 2028? We scored four sites of real interest to NASA, week by week,
and turned the results into clear tables, scores and a ranking that a non-expert can read in seconds.
details:
What it does
Lunar Site Advisor helps mission planners compare four Artemis III candidate landing regions at the lunar south pole (Malapert Massif, Haworth, Nobile Rim 1, de Gerlache Rim 2). It scores each site on two things: solar power potential and direct Earth communication. The results appear as simple tables, rankings and plain-language explanations.

How it works

  1. We analysed the first 7 days of every month of 2028, the period of NASA’s next planned missions and the length of a typical surface mission (12 windows per site).
  2. For Earth communication, we pulled hourly Earth elevation for each site’s coordinates from NASA JPL Horizons (168 samples per month, 2,016 per site). Earth counts as visible when it is above the horizon.
  3. For solar potential, we used Moon Trek and QuickMap (LRO/LOLA) illumination and terrain layers. [Team: add one line on how the solar score is computed.]
  4. Data was processed and combined into scores with Manus AI. The total score weights solar 60% and communication 40%, and each site is rated Good, Medium or Weak.

What works now (evidence)

  • Complete Earth-visibility results for all four sites and all 12 weeks of 2028. Malapert Massif is best (Earth visible about 80% of the time), then Nobile Rim 1 (78%), Haworth (75%) and de Gerlache Rim 2 (65%).
  • Clear calendar pattern: Earth is in view throughout January–March and September–November, and mostly hidden in May–July. October is fully visible at all four sites.
  • [Team: add the working features of the web interface, e.g. comparison table, month selector, charts.]

Benefits and goal
Planners get a fast, readable first comparison instead of reading several separate datasets. It shows which site and which month give reliable power and contact with Earth, and suggests better options when a site performs poorly. We hope it helps early mission planning and also helps students and the public understand why site choice matters.

Tools used
NASA JPL Horizons, Moon Trek, QuickMap (LRO/LOLA), CSA Moon Exploration portal, Manus AI (data processing and voice-over), Claude (proposal and tool structuring). [Team: add web stack, e.g. HTML/CSS/JavaScript and any 3D library.]

Limitations
Earth elevation is geometric, with no terrain blocking. Earth stays under about 10° above the horizon, so nearby hills could hide it at the exact landing point. Only the first week of each month is analysed. The 60/40 weighting is an adjustable assumption.

Future plans
Add the Shackleton comparison point, more sites and weeks, terrain-based horizon masking, and adjustable weights in the interface.
